question: In the Skill-Rule-Knowledge (SRK) model of behaviour, "skill-based" behaviour describes actions that are:

options.text: Impossible to perform without constant verbal instruction
Smooth, largely automatic and performed with little conscious thought, as with a well-practised manual flying technique
Entirely novel, requiring first-principles reasoning every time
Performed by reasoning through each step aloud, so the pilot must verbalise every control input before making it, which slows the whole task down considerably

explanation: Skill-based behaviour is the most automatic of the three levels: a highly practised action runs with minimal conscious monitoring, which frees attention for other things but, as noted elsewhere in this subject, also makes it a little more prone to slip-type errors.

question: "Rule-based" behaviour, the middle level of the SRK model, is applied when a person:

options.text: Recognises a familiar type of situation and applies a known procedure or rule learned for exactly that situation
Acts without any conscious recognition of the situation at all
Must invent an entirely new solution from basic principles
Has to decide on a response with no procedure available, reasoning through every possible option before acting on any of them

explanation: Rule-based behaviour sits between pure automatic skill and first-principles problem solving: the situation is recognised as a known type, and a stored rule or procedure (such as a checklist) that fits that type is applied — most of normal flying beyond the purely stick-and-rudder level works this way.

question: "Knowledge-based" behaviour, the highest level of the SRK model, is required when:

options.text: A task is being carried out in a familiar way, following a routine sequence that needs no fresh reasoning at any stage, and the pilot can usually describe each step from memory alone
A situation is genuinely novel and no practised skill or existing rule directly fits, requiring conscious, effortful reasoning from first principles
The situation is identical to one encountered the day before
A task is extremely well practised and fully automatic

explanation: Knowledge-based processing is the slowest, most effortful and most error-prone of the three levels, precisely because there is no ready-made rule or skill to fall back on — the person has to reason the problem through from scratch, which takes time and mental capacity a true emergency may not allow much of.

question: The three levels of the SRK model are useful for understanding error partly because:

options.text: Each level is prone to a different characteristic kind of error, so recognising which level a task sits at helps anticipate what is likely to go wrong
All three levels are equally fast and equally error-prone
Only knowledge-based behaviour can ever produce an error

The model was designed mainly to rank pilots by experience and has little bearing on how errors are classified, trained for or prevented, since it describes only aircraft systems and their maintenance schedules

explanation: Skill-based behaviour is prone to slips, rule-based behaviour is prone to misapplying a rule to a situation it does not really fit, and knowledge-based behaviour is prone to flawed reasoning under time pressure — three distinct failure modes that call for different safeguards.

question: Situational awareness is often described as having distinct levels, the most basic of which is:

options.text: Predicting what will happen several minutes into the future, based on the aircraft's current trend and the planned route ahead
Understanding what the perceived elements actually mean for the current situation
Predicting what will happen several minutes into the future
Perceiving the relevant elements in the environment — the raw facts, such as instrument readings, other traffic or terrain

explanation: The first and most basic level of situational awareness is simply noticing the relevant elements present — without perceiving the right information in the first place, no amount of later reasoning can build an accurate picture of the situation.

question: The second level of situational awareness, comprehension, goes beyond simply perceiving elements by:

options.text: Simply listing every instrument reading and radio call in sequence, with each item recorded but no attempt to link them together
Simply listing every instrument reading with no further interpretation
Occurring before any element has actually been perceived
Integrating and interpreting those elements to understand what they mean for the current situation as a whole

explanation: Comprehension is where isolated facts are combined into meaning — for example, recognising that a falling airspeed, a rising nose attitude and an aft trim position together mean an approach to a stall, rather than three unrelated readings.

question: The highest level of situational awareness, projection, refers to the ability to:

options.text: Anticipate how the situation is likely to develop in the near future, based on its current state and trend
Describing the situation only as it exists at this exact instant, without any reference to what has come before or what follows
Describe the situation only as it exists at this exact instant, with no reference to the future
Recall details from a flight that happened months ago

explanation: Projection is forward-looking: using the current, understood state of the situation to anticipate what is likely to happen next, which is what lets a crew act proactively (planning a diversion before fuel becomes critical, say) rather than only reactively.

question: A loss of situational awareness most often develops not as a single dramatic event but as:

options.text: Something that can only happen to inexperienced pilots
An instantaneous, all-or-nothing switch from fully aware to fully unaware
An instantaneous, all-or-nothing switch from fully aware to fully unaware, usually triggered by a single obvious warning that the crew cannot fail to notice in the cockpit at any time
A gradual drift, where the crew's mental picture slowly falls out of step with reality as small cues are missed or misinterpreted

explanation: Awareness usually erodes gradually, one missed cue or outdated assumption at a time, rather than failing all at once — which is why regularly cross-checking the picture against reality (a position check, a fuel check, a brief status review) matters even when nothing seems obviously wrong.

question: When evaluating incoming data (an instrument reading, a radio call, a warning light), a pilot's overall judgement benefits most from:

options.text: Cross-checking the data against other independent sources rather than accepting a single source at face value
Treating every single piece of information as equally certain and final
Treating every piece of information as equally certain and final, and acting on the first value shown without any further checks
Relying on a single sensor exclusively, regardless of what else is available

explanation: Any single sensor, instrument or report can be wrong. Cross-checking data against another independent source — a second altimeter, ATC confirmation, a visual cue — is the practical defence against building a picture of the situation on one faulty piece of information.

question: Intrinsic motivation, as distinct from extrinsic motivation, drives behaviour mainly through:

options.text: Satisfaction, interest or a sense of achievement found in the task itself, rather than an external reward or punishment
Factors that have nothing to do with a person's own attitude toward the task
Pay, promotion, bonuses or the threat of disciplinary action alone, with no personal interest in the task being performed, and no sense of achievement from doing it well at any stage
Pay, promotion or the threat of discipline alone

explanation: Intrinsic motivation comes from within — genuine interest, pride in doing the job well, enjoyment of flying itself — whereas extrinsic motivation is driven by outside incentives such as pay or avoiding punishment. Both can shape behaviour, often at the same time.

question: Strong external motivation to complete a flight (commercial pressure, a tight schedule, a desire not to disappoint passengers) is relevant to human performance mainly because it:

options.text: Always improves the objectivity of a pilot's decisions
Can bias a pilot's risk judgement toward continuing a flight or approach that, viewed more objectively, should be discontinued
Only ever affects decisions made on the ground, never in flight
Has no influence on decision making whatsoever, since pilots are trained to separate commercial pressure from every operational choice

explanation: This pattern — sometimes called plan continuation bias — reflects how motivation to achieve a goal (an on-time landing, a completed mission) can subtly weight a pilot's risk assessment toward continuing rather than discontinuing, even as evidence against continuing accumulates.

question: Complacency, in the human-factors sense, is best described as:

options.text: A healthy, justified confidence based on accurate, current information about the aircraft, the crew and the conditions ahead, which is reviewed again at each stage of the flight
A healthy, justified confidence based on accurate, current information
A false, unwarranted sense of confidence or security that reduces vigilance, often following a long period without any problem occurring
Something that can never develop during routine, uneventful flying

explanation: Complacency specifically describes confidence that has outrun the evidence — monitoring relaxes not because the situation has genuinely become safer, but because nothing has gone wrong for a while, which is exactly the condition under which an actual problem is most likely to be missed.

question: Complacency is particularly associated with highly automated or highly reliable systems because:

options.text: Automation makes complacency physically impossible, because the system continuously checks every decision the crew makes for them, so that no human monitoring is needed at all during flight
A long track record of the system working correctly can erode active monitoring, even though the system can still fail or be misconfigured
Complacency only ever affects manually flown tasks
Reliable systems require more active monitoring than unreliable ones, not less

explanation: Paradoxically, the more reliable a system has proven itself to be, the easier it becomes to stop actively verifying its output — exactly the dynamic that lets a rare automation failure or a subtle misconfiguration go unnoticed for longer than it otherwise would.

question: A pilot facing an unfamiliar emergency with no matching checklist is likely to find that correctly applying knowledge-based reasoning is made harder under high stress mainly because:

options.text: High stress narrows working memory and attention, which is exactly the capacity knowledge-based reasoning depends on most heavily
Stress only affects skill-based behaviour, never knowledge-based reasoning
Knowledge-based reasoning does not require working memory or attention at all
Knowledge-based reasoning does not require working memory or attention, so stress has no bearing on how well it is carried out, and experienced crews can always rely on it under pressure

explanation: Knowledge-based processing is the most demanding of the three SRK levels, relying heavily on working memory and flexible attention — exactly the resources that stress narrows and degrades, which is part of why a genuinely novel emergency under pressure is so difficult to manage well.

question: A crew briefing that explicitly states the plan, expected sequence of events and what would indicate a need to change course helps situational awareness mainly by:

options.text: Replacing the need for ongoing monitoring once the briefing is complete
Guaranteeing that nothing unexpected can ever happen during the flight
Guaranteeing that nothing unexpected can ever happen during the flight, so the crew need not watch for deviations once it starts, and any change to the plan can safely be left until later
Establishing a shared mental model in advance, which makes any later deviation from the plan easier for either crew member to notice and raise

explanation: A shared expectation of how the flight should unfold gives both crew members a common baseline to compare reality against, making a departure from the plan stand out to whichever of them notices it first, rather than only the one who happened to form that expectation privately.

question: A pilot who feels their work is unappreciated, poorly rewarded or going nowhere professionally may show reduced motivation that manifests, from a safety perspective, as:

options.text: Reduced diligence in routine but important tasks, such as thorough checklist use or careful pre-flight planning
No measurable change in behaviour of any kind
A condition that cannot be influenced by workplace factors
An automatic improvement in flying skill, as frustration sharpens attention and makes routine tasks feel more precise to perform

explanation: Motivation affects effort and diligence on exactly the routine, easy-to-skimp-on tasks that matter for safety — a demotivated person is more likely to cut corners on preparation and checking even while still being physically capable of flying the aircraft competently.

question: Simulator training for rare, high-risk emergencies is valuable partly because repeated practice:

options.text: Can shift the required response from slow, effortful knowledge-based reasoning toward faster, more reliable rule-based (or even skill-based) behaviour
Has no effect on which level of the SRK model a response falls under
Always makes a response purely knowledge-based, regardless of practice
Has no effect on which level of the SRK model a response falls under, since the level depends only on the aircraft type flown and the age of the pilot, not on how often a situation has been practised

explanation: What begins as effortful, error-prone, first-principles problem solving in an unfamiliar emergency can, through repeated deliberate practice, become a recognised, rule-based (or even largely skill-based) response — exactly why realistic, repeated simulator exposure to rare emergencies is considered so valuable.

question: Automation that quietly changes mode (for example, an autopilot reverting from one vertical mode to another) without being noticed is a classic cause of:

options.text: Improved situational awareness, since automation always improves understanding
A problem that can only occur with manual flying, never with automation

Improved situational awareness, since automation always improves understanding of what the aircraft is doing at every moment, so crews rarely need to check the mode annunciations or the flight director at all
A loss of situational awareness at the comprehension level, where the crew's understanding of "what the aircraft is doing" no longer matches reality

explanation: If a mode change is not perceived or correctly understood, the crew's mental model of what the automation is doing falls out of step with what it is actually doing — a comprehension-level breakdown in situational awareness that is a well-known hazard of complex automated systems.

question: "Garbage in, garbage out" is a phrase sometimes used to describe the risk that:

options.text: A decision can only be as good as the data it was based on, however sound the reasoning applied to that data was
This phrase applies only to computer systems, never to human decision making
Reasoning quality is the only factor that matters, so a sound thought process will always reach a correct decision regardless of the data
Reasoning quality is the only factor that matters, regardless of the data used

explanation: Even excellent judgement applied to wrong or outdated information produces a wrong conclusion. This is why evaluating the quality and currency of the data itself — not just the reasoning built on it — is part of good decision making.

question: A healthy level of motivation for safety-critical work is generally considered to be one that:

options.text: Has no relationship to safe decision making
Is as high as physically possible at all times, with no upper limit, since more drive to succeed always produces safer outcomes, and any hesitation to continue is a sign of weakness in the crew
Is as high as physically possible at all times, with no upper limit on how helpful it is
Drives diligence and care without becoming so strong a desire to succeed that it overrides sound judgement about when to stop or change plan

explanation: Motivation, like arousal, is not simply "more is better": enough to sustain diligence and care is valuable, but motivation strong enough to override a sound stop/divert decision becomes a risk in its own right, echoing the same inverted-U logic seen with arousal and performance.
